title: The Science of Cultural Spread: Networks, Attention, and Influence
summary: Memes do not spread because of one magic formula. Learn how content, social influence, networks, attention, and algorithms interact—and why popularity is not evidence of truth.

cover.alt: Two adult friends pass a glowing origami bird as differently coloured paper birds travel through a web of connected people and media.

blocks.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Memes do not spread because of one magic formula. Learn how content, social influence, networks, attention, and algorithms interact—and why popularity is not evidence of truth.

blocks.title: Warm-up

items.prompt: What is one idea, phrase, image, or habit that seemed to appear everywhere?
When many people share something, does that make you more likely to trust it? Why or why not?
Think of an online trend that changed as people copied it. What changed?

blocks.title: Part 1: A Meme Is More Than a Funny Picture
paragraphs: Today, a meme often means a captioned image or video that people copy and change online. To understand why ideas go viral, we can start with The Selfish Gene (1976), where Richard Dawkins proposed “meme” as a name for a unit of cultural transmission: an idea, tune, fashion, or practice that passes from person to person. His comparison with genes was powerful because it directed attention towards copying and survival. However, cultural information is not literally DNA. People can misunderstand it, combine it with other ideas, or deliberately redesign it. Modern cultural-evolution research therefore treats the gene comparison as a useful starting point, not a complete explanation of culture.

images.alt: Adults pass bird images from phone to phone while each version changes, beside an open book and a branching family of bird variations.

blocks.title: Check: Part 1: A Meme Is More Than a Funny Picture

items.prompt: Why is the gene comparison useful but incomplete?
items.answer: It focuses attention on copying and survival, but people actively interpret, combine, and change cultural information.

blocks.title: Part 2: Transmission, Variation, and Selection
paragraphs: Cultural evolution can be described through three linked processes. Transmission happens when information moves between people through speech, imitation, writing, teaching, or media. Variation appears when the information changes, either by accident or by design. Selection happens when some versions are copied or remembered more than others. Here, “selected” does not mean morally good, factually true, or biologically superior. It only means that one version became more common or lasted longer in a particular environment. A joke may become shorter because short versions are easier to retell. A recipe may become more detailed because accuracy matters to the cooks using it. Human goals shape each step.

blocks.title: Check: Part 2: Transmission, Variation, and Selection

items.prompt: In cultural evolution, what does it mean when a version is selected?
items.answer: It means that the version is copied or remembered more than competing versions in a particular environment.
items.explanation: Think of a popular phrase, recipe, fashion, or online meme. Which variation do you remember most, and why do you think it survived?

blocks.title: Part 3: We Choose What—and Whom—to Copy
paragraphs: Copying is not random. People may notice content because it is surprising, useful, frightening, funny, or easy to remember. They may also copy a person who seems respected or successful. In one narrative experiment, both the content of a story and the supposed prestige of its source influenced transmission; prestige mattered, but several content effects were stronger. Social information can then create a feedback loop. In a controlled online music experiment, 14,341 people chose songs by unknown bands. When participants could see earlier download numbers, popular songs became more unequal and final rankings became less predictable. Quality still had some influence, but early popularity helped create later popularity.

blocks.title: Check: Part 3: We Choose What—and Whom—to Copy

items.prompt: What did the music experiment show about social influence?
items.answer: Seeing earlier choices made popularity more unequal and final success less predictable, although song quality still mattered partly.

blocks.title: Part 4: Popularity and Truth Are Different Tests
paragraphs: A transmission test asks, “Will people pass this on?” A truth test asks, “Is the claim supported by reliable evidence?” These tests can produce different answers. A large study followed about 126,000 stories shared on Twitter from 2006 to 2017 and used six fact-checking organizations to classify them. In that dataset, false stories travelled farther, faster, deeper, and more broadly than true stories. The researchers also found that false news tended to be more novel. This does not prove that every false claim beats every true one, or that the same pattern exists on every platform. It shows why share counts cannot replace evidence.

blocks.title: Check: Part 4: Popularity and Truth Are Different Tests

items.prompt: Why can a high share count not serve as a truth test?
items.answer: Sharing measures transmission, while truth depends on the quality of evidence supporting a claim.
items.explanation: If a claim is popular but uncertain, what evidence would you want before passing it on?

blocks.title: Part 5: A Million Views May Not Be Viral
paragraphs: People often use “viral” to mean “very popular,” but network scientists can ask a more precise question: what shape did the spread take? Imagine two messages with one million views. A celebrity sends the first directly to a huge audience, creating a broadcast shaped like a star. The second passes through many generations: one person shares it, several recipients share it again, and new branches continue. Researchers call this second quality structural virality. After examining one billion diffusion events on Twitter, they found that popular events had many different shapes. However, structural virality was usually low, and a large broadcast often produced most of the popularity. Reach and person-to-person depth are not the same measurement.

images.alt: One central speaker sends orange paper birds directly to many people, while blue birds travel through a branching person-to-person chain.

blocks.title: Check: Part 5: A Million Views May Not Be Viral

items.prompt: What is the difference between a large broadcast and structurally viral spread?
items.answer: A broadcast reaches many people directly from a major source, while structurally viral spread continues through multiple generations of sharing.

blocks.title: Part 6: Some Ideas Need Reinforcement
paragraphs: The language of contagion is another model, not a claim that ideas are diseases. In a simple contagion, one contact may be enough to transmit information, as when you learn that a concert exists. A complex contagion requires reinforcement from several people before someone adopts a risky, costly, or uncertain behavior. Joining a protest, using an unfamiliar technology, or accepting a new group rule may work this way. In a randomized online experiment with 1,528 participants, a health behavior spread farther and faster through clustered networks than through random networks. Repeated social signals helped adoption. The result does not mean clustering always wins; it shows that the kind of decision changes which network structure is useful.

blocks.title: Check: Part 6: Some Ideas Need Reinforcement

items.prompt: Why might a complex contagion need several social contacts?
items.answer: A person may need repeated confirmation before adopting a behavior that feels risky, costly, uncertain, or socially unusual.
items.explanation: Which would probably need more reinforcement: hearing a new fact or changing a daily habit? What could change your answer?

blocks.title: Part 7: Clusters Reinforce; Bridges Carry
paragraphs: A network is a pattern of connections between people or groups. Dense clusters create repeated contact, shared expectations, and trust, so they can support complex adoption. Bridges connect different clusters and carry information into new communities. Yet one weak bridge may deliver a message without providing enough reinforcement for action. Complex-contagion theory therefore highlights bridge width: several independent links between groups may matter more than one long connection. There is no universally perfect network. Tight clusters can strengthen support but also trap an idea inside one group. Numerous bridges can increase reach but may weaken repeated confirmation. The outcome depends on what is spreading and what adoption requires.

blocks.title: Check: Part 7: Clusters Reinforce; Bridges Carry

items.prompt: Why can several links between groups be more useful than one link?
items.answer: Several links can carry the idea across groups while also providing the repeated confirmation that complex adoption may require.

blocks.title: Part 8: Attention and Algorithms Create a Selection Environment
paragraphs: People cannot inspect every message they receive. In one agent-based model, limited attention and network structure produced large differences in meme popularity even when the modeled items had equal quality. This does not prove that real ideas are equal; it reveals how competition for attention can magnify small accidents. Platforms add another layer by ranking what users see. A large randomized Twitter experiment found that an algorithmic timeline changed the relative visibility of political content compared with a reverse-chronological feed. Content matters too: in selected political discussions, moral-emotional language was associated with more sharing, especially inside ideological groups. That finding was observational, so it is not a universal recipe. Algorithms, human choices, and content interact in feedback loops.

blocks.title: Check: Part 8: Attention and Algorithms Create a Selection Environment

items.prompt: What does it mean to say that a platform creates a selection environment?
items.answer: Limited attention and ranking systems affect which items become visible, so some messages receive more opportunities to be copied than others.

blocks.title: Part 9: Use a Layered Model, Not a Viral Formula
paragraphs: No single feature explains why an idea takes over. A better analysis uses six layers. Content asks what the message says and how memorable it is. Mind asks what emotions, knowledge, and goals people bring. Source asks who communicates it and what social signals surround that person. Network asks how groups, clusters, and bridges are arranged. Time asks whether events and early accidents create an opportunity. Platform asks how interfaces and ranking distribute attention. These layers can also guide responsible communication. Make accurate information clear and easy to pass on, but keep the evidence attached. Build trusted connections across groups, but do not manufacture false popularity. The aim is not merely to win attention; it is to help valuable ideas travel without sacrificing truth.

images.alt: Two friends examine a glowing paper bird surrounded by connected scenes of message design, thought, trust, social groups, time, and phone selection.

blocks.title: Check: Part 9: Use a Layered Model, Not a Viral Formula

items.prompt: Why is a layered model better than a simple viral formula?
items.answer: It examines several interacting causes and avoids pretending that one feature guarantees popularity in every situation.

blocks.title: Final Reflection

items.prompt: Choose an idea that deserves wider attention. How would you improve its content, source, network path, timing, or platform presentation without weakening its truthfulness?
